GHSA-3cv6-jpf6-8222.summary: LiteLLM: Authenticated SSRF and provider-credential exfiltration via unvalidated request-body routing parameters
GHSA-3cv6-jpf6-8222.details:
### Impact

Any authenticated LiteLLM proxy user could redirect an outbound provider call to a destination they control and cause the proxy to send its own configured provider credentials to that destination. The proxy's request-body validation was a denylist that did not cover every sensitive parameter and did not inspect parameters nested inside other request fields, so a caller could supply a routing or credential value that the proxy applied without clearing the operator's stored key. Any authenticated user could therefore exfiltrate the operator's upstream provider credentials and other configured secrets, and perform Server-Side Request Forgery against internal services reachable from the proxy.

### Patches

Fixed in 1.96.2, 1.95.1, 1.94.3, 1.93.2, 1.92.2, 1.91.5, 1.90.7, 1.89.7, and 1.88.6.

### Workarounds

Set `general_settings.allow_client_side_credentials` to `false` so callers cannot override connection parameters, restrict proxy keys to trusted callers, and block the affected parameters (`api_base`, `base_url`, `model_list`, `fallbacks`, provider credential fields) at a reverse proxy or API gateway.

GHSA-5cjw-f85j-cv6r.summary: Tornado: Open redirect via triple-slash redirect paths
GHSA-5cjw-f85j-cv6r.details:
### Summary

Due to differences in the way browsers and Python's `urllib` parse urls, browsers treat a string starting with three or more slashes as a protocol-level redirect, while `urllib` does not. This means that the 6.6.0 fix for the RedirectHandler open redirect (CVE-2026-116578, commit cc75ab0e) is incomplete. Tornado 6.6.1 improves the open-redirect detection to handle this case correctly, as well as fixing a regression in the 6.6.0 implementation.

GHSA-g5ff-637f-6q2m.summary: LiteLLM: internal_user_viewer arbitrary local file read via `vertex_ai_credentials`
GHSA-g5ff-637f-6q2m.details:
## Summary

An authenticated LiteLLM proxy user could read arbitrary local files from the proxy runtime by sending a crafted `vertex_ai_credentials` value to `/utils/transform_request`. The request-body safety blocklist rejected `vertex_credentials` but missed its alias `vertex_ai_credentials`, which let the value reach the Vertex AI credential loader and trigger a file read that is sent to an attacker-controlled URL.

## Impact

A low-privilege authenticated user (only `internal_user_viewer`, obtainable through SSO login on many deployments) could read any file readable by the LiteLLM process. Reading files such as `/proc/self/environ` can disclose `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` and provider API keys, so the impact can escalate to full proxy-admin control.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `1.95.0` or later. The fix adds the missing alias to the request-body blocklist, so no configuration change is needed once you upgrade. There is no reliable configuration workaround on affected versions.

GHSA-mmhr-3c5m-f64f.summary: Soup Sieve: Polynomial-time denial of service in the descendant combinator
GHSA-mmhr-3c5m-f64f.details:
## Summary

Matching a selector that uses the descendant combinator (`a b`) takes time that grows polynomially with how deeply the document is nested, and each extra descendant combinator in the selector raises the degree by one. A selector with `k` descendant combinators takes `O(n^(k+1))` time on a chain of `n` nested elements.

An attacker who controls the HTML or XML that an application passes to Soup Sieve (directly, or through Beautiful Soup's `select()`, `select_one()`, `css.select()`, etc.) can send a very small, deeply nested document that keeps a CPU busy for seconds to minutes against an ordinary selector such as `section div div`.

## Details

To match `a b`, Soup Sieve checks each element against `b` and then walks up through its ancestors looking for one that matches `a`. When the selector has more descendant combinators, the rest of the selector is tried again from each ancestor on that walk, and so on for every combinator. Nothing was reused between walks, so the same ancestors were matched against the same part of the selector over and over.

The worst case is when the leftmost part of the selector never matches, as in `section div div` against a document of nested `<div>` with no `<section>`: every walk goes all the way to the root and no search can stop early.

### Timings

Example timings with `html.parser` on Soup Sieve 3.0.4 and 4.0, using a document of nested `<div>` (5 bytes each) and no matches:

| Nesting depth | Input size | Selector | 3.0.4 | 4.0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2,000 | 10 KB | `section div` | 1.6 s | 0.05 s |
| 4,000 | 20 KB | `section div` | 5.1 s | 0.01 s |
| 400 | 2 KB | `section div div` | 6.7 s | < 0.01 s |
| 800 | 4 KB | `section div div` | 53.0 s | < 0.01 s |
| 100 | 0.5 KB | `section div div div` | 2.5 s | < 0.01 s |
| 200 | 1 KB | `section div div div` | 40.9 s | < 0.01 s |

None of these selectors use unusual syntax.

## Proof of concept

```py
import time
import bs4
import soupsieve as sv

soup = bs4.BeautifulSoup('<div>' * 200, 'html.parser')
t = time.process_time()
sv.select('section div div div', soup)
print(time.process_time() - t)
```

On affected versions, doubling the nesting depth multiplies the time by about 2^(k+1), where `k` is the number of descendant combinators: about 4x for `section div`, 8x for `section div div`, and 16x for `section div div div`.

## Impact

Applications are affected if they run selectors with descendant combinators against documents that untrusted users can influence, such as scrapers, HTML sanitizers or filters, and services that process uploaded or fetched markup. Descendant combinators are among the most common parts of CSS selectors, and a document of about 1 KB is enough to tie up a worker for close to a minute. Applications that only run selectors against trusted documents are not affected.

## Patches

Fixed in 4.0 by [facelessuser/soupsieve#351](https://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/pull/351). Whether an element is, or has an ancestor that is, a match for part of a selector depends only on its parent, so Soup Sieve now caches that result per element and relation for every element visited on the walk. Each descendant combinator is then linear in the size of the document. Results are unchanged, and ordinary documents are no slower.

Caching is enabled by default, so no changes are needed beyond upgrading. The `NOCACHE` flag is a temporary fallback for users who run into problems with caching, and it is planned for removal. It uses the old uncached matching, so selectors compiled with `NOCACHE` are still subject to polynomial time and shouldn't be used with descendant combinators on untrusted input.

## Workarounds

If users can't upgrade:

- Use as few descendant combinators as they can in selectors that run on untrusted documents. Where the structure of the
  document is known, the child combinator (`a > b`) only looks at the parent and is not affected.
- Limit the size and nesting depth of untrusted documents before selecting on them.
- Run selection on untrusted input with a time limit, for example in a worker process that can be stopped.

GHSA-vvf4-9x63-8xvv.summary: dnspython has excessive memory and CPU use
GHSA-vvf4-9x63-8xvv.details:
### Summary

A maliciously crafted zone file could use a WKS record to consume excessive memory and CPU, possibly causing the process to exit due to memory exhaustion.

### Details

The `from_text()` parser does not check that a WKS record service number is between 0 and 65535 inclusive.  It then uses this number to resize the bitmap to accommodate a bit with that offset.  This can cause extremely large memory allocations, and also extends the array very inefficiently, wasting CPU.

### Proof of concept

This demonstrates the failure to limit the service number, though with a value that does not cause excessive memory or CPU consumption.

```
rd = dns.rdata.from_text("IN", "WKS", "10.0.0.1 udp 65536")
```

### Impact

If dnspython is used to read zonefile format where the attacker can control the type and rdata text, the program may consume excessive memory or CPU, denying service.
